summary: Observation of a large triangular shape with very bright lights
description: On December 22, 2001, at approximately 2:30 a.m., a witness in a car observed a large triangular shape flying slowly and silently. After stopping his vehicle, the witness got out and noted that the object hovered above him for about ten seconds before moving on. Beneath the object were very bright, rapidly moving lights; the front of the object appeared to be made of plexiglass. The investigation revealed that the witness's personality made his testimony less credible.

On December 1, 2001, at approximately 11:40 PM, several witnesses observed the passage of 6 to 12 very bright points of light for about fifteen seconds, which then burned out rapidly. This was probably an atmospheric reentry.
On October 21, 2001, at approximately 5:40 a.m., a witness observed a saucer-shaped light rotating on its axis for about ten seconds. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of the probable reentry of an object into the atmosphere.
description: On October 7, 2001, at approximately 7:30 PM, several independent witnesses observed the very rapid passage of a green fireball accompanied by bright white points with trails. This was likely the re-entry of an object into the atmosphere.

summary: Observation of a long, stationary transparent tube and sudden disappearance: lack of information.
description: In 2008, a witness reported an observation made on October 5, 2001: the witness, while hunting, observed a long, transparent tube in the sky for a few minutes, undulating in the wind. Initially thinking it was an optical illusion, the witness was intrigued when the object suddenly disappeared. No other reports were collected about this phenomenon. The described object resembled a thermal (solar) balloon. However, due to a lack of precise information, this case is classified as "C".

summary: Observation of the rapid passage of a triangular shape.
description: During the night of September 26-27, at 2:14 AM, a witness observed a large, triangular object passing rapidly by for 7 to 10 seconds. This object, which appeared much larger than an airplane, moved silently and very quickly, approximately two to three times faster than an airplane, at an estimated altitude of 600 to 700 meters. The triangular shape was dark, with a phosphorescent light at each end. No explanation could be found for this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of circles of charred grass on a football field: no observation of an aerospace phenomenon: unusable testimony.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named TOUSSUS LE NOBLE (78) 07.09.2001, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On September 7, 2001, on the football field in Villiers-Le-Bacle (91), the prefect's representative discovered three circles of charred grass, each approximately 30 to 40 cm in diameter, forming an isosceles triangle roughly 120 meters long. The gendarmerie investigation uncovered charcoal dumped in a nearby pit and numerous vehicle tracks, evidence of the recent occupation of the adjacent land by travelers. GEIPAN (at the time, SEPRA) classified the case as unexplained. GEIPAN no longer investigates sightings that do not include an aerospace phase, meaning sightings perceived by the witness as having been (at least during one phase of the observation) in the sky or in the immediate vicinity of the sky and the ground. It is in the aerospace field that GEIPAN possesses the expertise and tools to investigate explanations for aerospace phenomena. Ground traces are, of course, used and are valuable when they are associated or can be associated with an aerospace observation. This is absolutely not the case here; there is no UFO testimony. Consequently, the testimony must be declared unusable by GEIPAN: case classified as C.

summary: Passage of a triangle delimited by three bright points in the sky: lack of information.
description: On August 20, 2001, at approximately 11:15 PM, a witness at a campground observed a triangular object, delimited by three points of light, passing across the sky. The phenomenon was silent and lasted a few minutes. The witness's son tried unsuccessfully to film it. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of the passage of 3 bright points
description: On August 12, 2001, at approximately 2:15 a.m., a couple observing shooting stars witnessed three bright orange lights that passed over them for about ten seconds. The witness, an air traffic controller, estimated the altitude at 10,000 feet and the speed at 500 knots. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of the passage of an object the size of an airplane with a dull thud.
description: On July 4, 2001, at approximately 10:30 PM, witnesses observed an object the size of a DC-10 airplane with a row of yellow lights flying quite low and making a muffled noise. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of a bright cylindrical object moving slowly
description: On June 24, 2001, at approximately 7:00 PM, a witness observed a slowly moving, vertical cylindrical object. The witness filmed the phenomenon, following it on a motorcycle to get a better view of its movements. The object's estimated altitude was 600 meters, and it appeared to be 15 meters high and 2.5 meters in diameter. It was aluminum-colored with bright spots resembling headlights. Its movement was slow, estimated at about 10 km/h. The investigation failed to identify the object.

summary: Probable observation of the planet Mars
description: On June 22, 2001, at approximately 9:30 PM, witnesses observed a very bright point of light in the sky moving very slowly towards the north-northwest. This was likely an astronomical observation, probably the planet Mars.

summary: Probable sighting of a decoy dropped by a military aircraft.
description: On June 6, 2001, at 4:40 PM, the crew of an A300 flying to Toulouse observed a fast-moving, incandescent light phenomenon on a descending trajectory. Given the proximity of a military zone, the sighting was likely identified as a flare dropped by a military aircraft. The phenomenon was also observed by the crew of another aircraft.

summary: Observation of a probable atmospheric reentry
description: On April 30, 2001, at 5:35 a.m., the crew of a DC-10 bound for Bordeaux observed a green glow passing by for 3 to 4 seconds, following a downward trajectory, probably due to atmospheric reentry. The observation was made at an estimated distance of over 10 km.

On the night of March 31st to April 1st, 2001, and again the following night, several witnesses observed a bright point larger than a star. When observed through binoculars, colored sparkles appeared within the point of light. The phenomenon was silent and remained visible for several hours. It is likely that these observations were of particularly bright stars.

summary: Observation of the probable reentry of an object into the atmosphere.
description: On March 13, 2001, at approximately 7:50 PM, a witness observed the passage of a very bright point of light with a luminous trail. As the witness immediately interpreted, this was likely the re-entry of an object into the atmosphere.

On January 7, 2001, at approximately 7:00 PM, a witness observed three bright lights in the sky. These lights were initially stationary and silent, then moved slowly to the left, accompanied by two flashing lights, one red and one white. The observation lasted approximately four minutes. No further information is available (direct testimony, no police investigation).

summary: Simultaneous observations from two watchtowers in France and Spain of a stationary luminous phenomenon in the sky: astronomical observations of Capella.
description: It's routine for Emma in the Biarritz-Parma control tower on the morning of January 16, 2001. Day breaks and the sky is clear. Around 7:45 a.m., the phone rings. It's her colleague Jose from the San Sebastian Fuenterrabía control tower who has observed a fixed point of light above the sea and is trying to find out if the observation is confirmed in Biarritz. Indeed, the phenomenon is detected, although no radar detection is recorded. The observed light is flickering, and faced with this suspicious phenomenon, the two controllers, who remain in telephone contact, each apply the security procedures planned for this situation. Jose, the Spanish air traffic controller, calls the Madrid air traffic control, which confirms there is no air traffic in the area, then the Bilbao military air traffic control, which gives the same answer. However, a plot is registered by the Torrejon radar control. Is it the same phenomenon? For her part, Emma conducted similar investigations with air traffic control in Bordeaux, which observed nothing, as did the military personnel, who were also questioned. The phenomenon disappeared after about half an hour. All this information was transmitted the same day by fax to SEPRA, which in turn contacted the CCOA in Taverny. The latter detected nothing unusual but sought confirmation of the unknown radar detection made by the military personnel in Torrejon. They denied it shortly afterward. Within CNES itself, a verification was launched to identify a possible balloon launch from the center in Aire-sur-l'Adour. Here again, the result was negative, and the observation remained a mystery. A decision was then made to investigate on-site on February 2, 2001. The head of SEPRA interviewed the two witnesses in Biarritz and San Sebastian, and they carried out a reconstruction and took measurements. These theodolite readings provide crucial information. Indeed, the observation direction of the phenomenon is identical as seen from Biarritz and San Sebastian, which are approximately 40 km apart. The observed phenomenon is therefore very distant and cannot be explained by an aircraft. This case will be classified as B by SEPRA: probable astronomical observation. RE-EXAMINATION OF THE CASE: GEIPAN continues to publish all of its archives on its public website www.geipan.fr. Its publications include older cases, initially classified as type B, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. This observation case was classified as eB in 2001 by SEPRA. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the past few years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This case is consistent (two witnesses, both air traffic controllers), and the description of the observed UFO is very precise. The sincerity and credibility of the witnesses have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the star Capella, which exhibited exceptional scintillation due to particular atmospheric conditions. It is not the visual perception of the witnesses that is in question, but rather their interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (astonishment, nighttime observation, unusual scintillation). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as PAN A, an observation linked to a misunderstanding with the star Capella.
